The Period of the Rise of Islam
This situation led to the institution of brotherhood between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Calling this “brotherhood” a form of legislation means that it was not introduced merely as an abstract moral or humanitarian principle. It was a practical social arrangement designed to deal with a real but temporary situation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The emigrants arrived from Mecca after being driven from their homes. Some had already been poor. Others had been wealthy but had been forced to leave Mecca with nothing.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
They therefore arrived in Medina without the means to provide themselves with housing or food.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The system of “brotherhood” established by Islam was an urgent and necessary way of giving them shelter and support. But they were not treated simply as refugees living in the homes of the Anṣār. They were treated as their “brothers” in faith, with rights of housing and support similar to those of brothers by blood and family.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It was meant to remain in force only as long as the emergency that had made it necessary continued. Once that need disappeared, the law itself would disappear.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
When the circumstances that the law had been created to address came to an end, the system of “brotherhood” was abrogated.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Those circumstances began to disappear when war booty from successful attacks on Quraysh’s caravans started flowing to the Muslims. The Muhājirūn could then support themselves instead of depending on the Anṣār.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The abrogation of the law of “Islamic brotherhood” in this way was the first practical example of something important in Islamic legislation: an implicit recognition of the law of development and change.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Abrogation assumes that a law exists because an objective need calls for it. The law comes into force because that need exists, and it remains in force only as long as the need remains.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The second is that this principle also recognizes that the need behind a law can change as objective circumstances change. No need is permanently fixed, because the conditions that create it are themselves not fixed.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
We will return to this subject in later chapters.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This second type of legislation rested on the following basis.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At the time Islam appeared, a society built increasingly around commercial relations was developing, and its material base was growing.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

This development required the old tribal structures and loyalties to be broken down. The human groups living along trade routes and in commercial centers had to be brought together within a single social framework: one institution, or, in other words, one unified state.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At that time, Islam as law and social order was uniquely suited to provide this framework—to become this institution, or this “state.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This historical task necessarily required a legal foundation and a complete system of general laws.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Some of these laws dealt with circumstances that already existed. Others dealt with situations expected to arise as the new society took shape.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
In this setting, there had to be laws governing fighting under the banner of Islam so that Islam could win and spread.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

These had to be accompanied by laws governing grants and war booty, laws concerning lands conquered either by force or by treaty, and laws dealing with the many new situations created—or expected to be created—by the Arab-Islamic conquests both inside and outside the Arabian Peninsula.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This body of legislation served two closely connected purposes.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam

The second may even have been more immediately effective, because these laws created material incentives to take part in conquest and expansion beyond the barren peninsula. Those incentives added material enthusiasm to the religious enthusiasm of the believers who fought in the armies of conquest.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The same laws also served a third purpose, this time involving consciousness.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

A person who had lived in the pre-Islamic age did not instantly lose the ways of thinking formed in that earlier society simply by entering the Islamic age. Those older habits of memory and thought remained until a new Islamic consciousness became firmly established.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

And that new consciousness could take root only through actual participation in the new Islamic society. By living and acting within this new historical setting, people gradually formed a new kind of social memory.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
This gives the legislation we have been discussing another function.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Among Muslims taking part in expansion under the banner of Islam, it helped establish a clear understanding of what they were doing—what we might call the unifying “theory” behind their actions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That theory rested on the following principles:
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Fighting for one common, unifying institution instead of fighting the fragmenting and destructive wars of rival tribes.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Fighting in ways intended to develop human capacities and widen the fields in which people could use them, instead of exhausting those capacities in cycles of personal, family, and tribal revenge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Turning the right of revenge from a right belonging to the individual or the tribe into a right belonging to society and its common institution.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Changing revenge from an act of personal, family, or tribal retaliation into a social punishment intended to defend the interests of society as a whole.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
On this basis, organized warfare was established as a tool either for expanding the authority of the social, political, and ideological institution or for protecting that institution.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Islamic legislation also changed the legal basis of social organization.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Tribal customs and Bedouin traditions, which reflected the old subsistence economy, had previously formed the main “legal” foundation of society.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But the new society of commercial and social relations needed a different kind of legal foundation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Islamic legislation was an objective response to this development.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Under the religious authority of Islam as law, a new legal order emerged. It included the idea of the “state” and the idea of an organized system of “law.”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The general rules of Islamic law therefore became a body of laws governing society as a whole, with everyone subject to decisions made under them.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Bedouin traditions had not recognized any authority beyond the boundaries of a particular tribe or its own customs.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Islam now made the authority of its law the one supreme authority above all others.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
D — Intellectual Debate and the Relationship Between Knowledge and Faith
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Islam’s position on intellectual debate can only be understood in relation to its position on knowledge. The question of knowledge lies at the root of the whole issue.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
There are two main questions here.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
First: where does human knowledge come from?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Second: how far can human beings go in gaining knowledge through their own powers of understanding?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
If we approach the question only by looking at the relationship between knowledge and religious faith, we might conclude that Islam recognizes only one source of knowledge: God.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That would mean denying the ability of reason, or any other human faculty, to gain knowledge independently.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Such a conclusion might seem to follow from the fact that Islam presents divine revelation as the source of its message.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Both doctrine and law come from revelation. And Islam’s account of the world, in the details it provides, also comes from revelation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Prophet communicates what is revealed to him: “The Messenger’s duty is only to deliver the message” (Qurʾān 5:99). God alone, by His will, chose him to communicate it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The foundations of belief and the rules of Islamic law are themselves forms of knowledge.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

If this knowledge comes from God, and from God alone, then it might seem to follow that knowledge about the origin of the world, the problems of existence, and the laws of nature, society, and thought does not come from the human faculties of understanding or from their interaction with the world we experience through the senses.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
If that were the case, then faith in the Islamic message would require people simply to accept this knowledge completely.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
There would be neither a right nor an ability to debate it, because debate involves doubt, while faith appears to exclude doubt.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Our first conclusion, then, might be that Islam rejects intellectual debate.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
We will now see how far that conclusion reflects the actual situation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
At first sight, some Islamic texts—the Qurʾān and the hadith—seem to support it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
“If they argue with you, say: ‘God knows best what you do. God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning the matters over which you differed.’” (Qurʾān 22:68–69)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
“They ask you about the spirit. Say: ‘The spirit belongs to my Lord’s command, and you have been given only a little knowledge.’” (Qurʾān 17:85)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
“No one knows its interpretation except God. Those firmly grounded in knowledge say: ‘We believe in it; it all comes from our Lord.’” (Qurʾān 3:7)
The Period of the Rise of Islam
There is also a hadith reported by Jābir.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

“Surāqa ibn Khathʿam came and said: ‘Messenger of God, explain our religion to us as though we had just been created. What are our actions based on now? On what the pens have already written and destiny has already decided, or on what still lies ahead?’
The Period of the Rise of Islam
He replied: ‘No. Rather, on what the pens have already written and destiny has already decided.’
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Surāqa asked: ‘Then what is the point of acting?’
The Period of the Rise of Islam
He replied: ‘Act. Each person is made ready for what he was created for, and every person acts according to his work.’”
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Period of the Rise of Islam
It deals with divine decree and destiny—in other words, with the question of whether human beings have freedom of will or whether their actions are predetermined.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Surāqa, who according to the hadith was one of the Prophet’s companions, asks a direct question.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Are our actions determined by what has already been written for us—by what the pens of the unseen world wrote before they dried, meaning that the matter has already been decided?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Or do we act according to choices we ourselves make about the future course of our lives?
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Prophet replies, according to the hadith, that people act according to what has already been written for them and has become part of their destiny.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
Each person is “made ready for what he was created for.” In other words, each person is bound by what was assigned to him from the beginning of creation.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
People are simply told to act, without continuing to question the matter, and each person will receive the reward or punishment for his actions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The hadith therefore has two important implications.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The first is that one of the Prophet’s companions wanted to understand a question connected with the way people act in their individual and social lives.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
He asked the Prophet about it.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
The Prophet referred human affairs back to destiny and then brought the discussion to an end, telling people to leave the matter to God, who would judge each person according to his actions.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
From this, we might conclude that knowledge of everything ultimately refers back to what has been written by divine destiny, leaving no room for debate.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But the hadith has a second implication.
The Period of the Rise of Islam

Although the companions had been taught that knowledge came from God through revelation and was to be accepted rather than debated, we can already see someone among them wanting to move beyond the habit of simply receiving knowledge through unquestioning acceptance.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
That desire appeared in the form of a question containing at least the beginnings of a discussion.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
But the old habit of simply accepting what was given quickly brought the attempt to an end, and the debate stopped.
The Period of the Rise of Islam
